bigFile.title: Large file size ({size})
bigFile.detail: Large PNG files bloat the repository and lengthen Unity import times. The suggestions below aim to reduce this size.

noAlpha.title: Alpha channel is not used
noAlpha.detail: All pixels are fully opaque (alpha = 255), but the file is saved as {colorType}. Removing alpha turns each pixel from 4 bytes into 3 bytes. Pixel values do not change.

hiddenRgb.title: Hidden color data in transparent pixels should be cleaned
hiddenRgb.detail: About {pct} of the {count} fully transparent pixels contain invisible RGB data. This data hurts compression; zeroing it does not change the appearance.

faint.title: Faint alpha values (1–3): {pct}
faint.detail: These pixels have alpha between 1 and 3 and are practically invisible. The "Faint alpha (1–3) → 0" variant sets them to 0 automatically; still check soft edges visually.

partial.title: Heavy partial alpha ({pct})
partial.detail: Many semi-transparent pixels (soft edges, shadows, antialiasing). Palette quantization may produce more visible artifacts on such images; check the quality table.

manyColors.title: {count} distinct colors: a 256-color palette can be tried as lossy
manyColors.noQuality: Palette quality could not be measured.

fewColors.title: Color count {count} (≤ 256): an indexed PNG may apply
fewColors.detail: The colors fit a 256-entry palette. An indexed PNG may be lossless; check the quality table.

grayscale.title: All visible pixels are grayscale
grayscale.detail: R=G=B for every pixel. A grayscale PNG (single channel) can be smaller; in Unity it can be used as a separate grayscale texture.

metadata.title: Unnecessary metadata: {list}
metadata.detail: Color profiles and text chunks are usually not used in games. The lossless optimized output does not write them.

maxSize.title: Above the Unity default Max Size ({max}): {w}×{h}
maxSize.detail: Unity downsizes the texture according to Max Size on import. Producing output at the size actually displayed saves both file size and memory.

npot.title: Dimensions are not powers of two
npot.detail: Unity supports NPOT textures; still, powers of two (e.g. 1024, 2048) suit mipmaps and some compression formats better.

losslessSaving.title: Lossless optimization saves {saving} ({pct})
losslessSaving.detail: Size {before} → {after}. Pixel values are unchanged; alpha cleanup and oxipng were applied.

unity.body: Unity converts PNG to a texture format on import. Runtime memory depends mainly on texture resolution and the Compression setting, not on file size. File size reductions help the repository and import; for memory, set Max Size to what is actually displayed.

blocks.summary: How is the raw pixel data calculated?
blocks.html:
In an 8-bit RGBA image every pixel stores 4 bytes (red, green, blue, alpha). For example an image of 1831 × 2572 px has about 4.7 million pixels → uncompressed about 4.7 M × 4 = 18 MB.

PNG compresses this data with DEFLATE. Repeated areas (flat color, repeated patterns) shrink a lot; but noisy data with a different color on every pixel (paper texture, antialiased edges) does not compress well.

Alpha stores how opaque each pixel is: 255 fully opaque, 0 fully transparent, values in between semi-transparent.

  • Fully opaque means unnecessary: the alpha channel can be removed; each pixel becomes 3 bytes instead of 4.
  • Transparent pixels: the RGB value of a pixel with alpha = 0 is never visible. It still takes space in the file and hurts compression. Zeroing it does not change the appearance (lossless).
  • Partial alpha: needed for soft edges, shadows and antialiasing. Changing these values changes the edges.

An indexed PNG stores each pixel as a 1-byte index and keeps the colors in a palette table of up to 256 entries. If the image has 256 colors or fewer this is lossless; if it has more, the colors are approximated by quantization (libimagequant). That is lossy.

The coverage curve shows that a few most-used colors cover most pixels. If the curve rises quickly, the palette loss is small.

• Lossless: every pixel stays exactly the same. Only the storage format and compression change (alpha removal, zeroing transparent RGB, oxipng).
  • Lossy: some pixels change (palette). It is measured with PSNR and maximum color difference; the final decision should be made with a visual check.

Before each row PNG stores a filter type (None, Sub, Up, Average, Paeth). Filters reduce differences between neighboring pixels; DEFLATE then encodes repetitions.

oxipng searches for the best filter and compression settings for each row. The result is lossless: the image does not change, it only uses fewer bytes. Higher levels are slower.

PSNR (dB) measures the error between the original and the result on a logarithmic scale; higher means more similar. Rule of thumb: 45 dB and above is usually indistinguishable to the eye; below 38 dB distortion can be visible. These thresholds are not exact; gradients and soft shadows make loss easier to notice.

blocks.summary: Does the PNG file size directly decide game memory?
blocks.html:
No. When importing, Unity decodes the PNG and converts it to the texture format you choose (e.g. RGBA32, ASTC, DXT). Runtime memory depends on that format and on the texture size (px); the PNG compression in the file does not directly change game memory.

The file size savings show up in: the project repository (Git), project folder size, import time and sometimes pre-build processing time.

The main lever for memory: the Max Size and Compression settings in Import Settings, and the resolution that is actually needed.

blocks.summary: What to watch in Import Settings
blocks.html:
• Max Size: do not go above the size displayed on screen.
  • Generate Mip Maps: usually off for UI and 2D sprites.
  • Alpha Is Transparency: keep on only for images that really use semi-transparency.
  • Read/Write Enabled: keep off unless needed (it creates a CPU copy in memory).
